about: Launch-vehicle reference data for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator mission step. First-order comparison data, not for mission design. Capability to trans-lunar injection (TLI) depends on the vehicle configuration, launch site, fairing and trajectory: every figure states the configuration it refers to and whether it is a published number or an estimate made for this tool.

tli_basis_legend.published: Figure read from the operator's own web page during the November 2026 check.
tli_basis_legend.published-secondary: Operator/agency figure as quoted by a secondary source (Wikipedia infobox) during the November 2026 check; the primary document was not opened.
tli_basis_legend.estimate: Not published. Estimated for this tool; method stated per vehicle. Expect roughly +/-20% error.
tli_basis_legend.refuelling-model: No direct TLI figure. Depends on in-orbit propellant transfer; modelled as a number of tanker flights (estimate range).
tli_basis_legend.leo-only: Launcher delivers to low Earth orbit only; the tool adds a TLI burn by the spacecraft's own stage at the entered Isp.

estimate_method: GTO-scaling estimate: m_TLI = (m_GTO + m_dry) * exp(-dV / (g0 * Isp)) - m_dry, with dV = 0.677 km/s (TLI 3.131 km/s minus GTO 2.455 km/s, both from a 200 km circular orbit, vis-viva) and assumed upper-stage dry mass m_dry and Isp. Checked against vehicles with published TLI figures: Vulcan VC6 11.7 t vs 11.5 t published, Ariane 64 9.0 t vs 8.6 t, LVM3 2.9 t vs 3.0 t, New Glenn 8.1 t vs 7.0 t, Long March 5 11.2 t vs 8.8-9.4 t. So the method can be 5-25% optimistic.

launchers.name: SLS Block 1
launchers.config: Block 1: core + 2 five-segment boosters + ICPS upper stage
launchers.status_note: 2 launches, 2 successes: Artemis I (16 Nov 2022) and Artemis II (crewed lunar flyby, launched 1 Apr 2026, splashdown 10 Apr 2026). Programme restructured in Feb-Mar 2026: Block 1B, Block 2 and the Exploration Upper Stage were cancelled; a ULA Centaur V-derived upper stage replaces ICPS for the lunar missions from 2028 (sources differ on whether that starts with Artemis IV or V; no TLI figure published for that configuration). Artemis III (2027) is now a low-Earth-orbit docking test. SLS is a government vehicle flown for Artemis/Orion, not a launcher that can be bought for another payload.
launchers.tli_note: Block 1 with ICPS: >27 t to TLI (NASA figure as quoted by Wikipedia; NASA's own fact-sheet PDF could not be opened during the check).

launchers.name: Starship
launchers.config: Block 3 (V3) Super Heavy + Ship, refuelled in low Earth orbit
launchers.status_note: 14 integrated flights to 28 Sep 2026. First Block 3 (V3) flight 22 May 2026 (suborbital). Flight 14 (28 Sep 2026) entered Earth orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Ship-to-ship propellant transfer has NOT been demonstrated; SpaceX plans to attempt it in early 2027. Any lunar use depends on that.
launchers.leo_note: Block 3 design figure (reusable), not yet demonstrated at this mass
launchers.tli_note: No published TLI figure. Modelled here as: the Ship carries the lander stack to LEO, is refuelled by tanker flights, performs the TLI burn itself and is expended. Tanker count is an estimate range from assumed (unverified) ship dry mass and Isp.
launchers.lunar_heritage: None yet (selected as an Artemis crewed lander, HLS)

refuel.ship_dry_basis: ASSUMPTION, unverified: SpaceX has not published a Block 3 ship dry mass
refuel.ship_isp_basis: ASSUMPTION, unverified: representative vacuum methane/oxygen value
refuel.prop_capacity_basis: about 1,200 t quoted for the lunar-lander variant (newspaceeconomy.ca, 9 Nov 2026)
refuel.tanker_payload_basis: 100-120 t per tanker is the SpaceX baseline, 150 t is an Elon Musk projection (same article); neither demonstrated
refuel.loss_allowance_basis: ASSUMPTION: +30% propellant for boil-off, transfer losses and reserves at the pessimistic end of the range
refuel.published_hls_estimates: For comparison, published estimates for a full crewed Starship HLS landing (the Ship itself lands, so it is filled completely): 6-8 refuelling flights (Elon Musk), about 10 (SpaceX executives, 2024), 10-14 (SpaceX baseline), 16 launches (GAO, from the 2021 proposal), 'high teens' (NASA, Nov 2023), about 22 (an Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel member, Oct 2026).

launchers.name: Falcon Heavy
launchers.status_note: 12 launches, all successful; latest ViaSat-3 F3 on 29 Apr 2026. Recovering the boosters lowers performance substantially (GTO 26.7 t expendable vs 8 t with all three cores recovered).
launchers.tli_note: No TLI figure published. Estimate by GTO scaling from the advertised 26.7 t to GTO (expendable), assuming a 4.5 t upper-stage dry mass and Isp 348 s (assumptions) -> about 21 t. The same method reproduces the advertised 16.8 t to Mars within about 3%. Mission-specific performance is likely lower.
launchers.lunar_heritage: None flown; Astrobotic Griffin Mission One is manifested

launchers.name: Falcon 9
launchers.status_note: The most-flown operational launcher. With a drone-ship landing the same estimate gives about 3.7 t to TLI (from 5.5 t to GTO).
launchers.tli_note: No TLI figure published. Estimate by GTO scaling from the advertised 8.3 t to GTO (expendable), assuming a 4.5 t upper-stage dry mass and Isp 348 s (assumptions) -> about 6.0 t. The same method reproduces the advertised 4.02 t to Mars within about 2%.
launchers.lunar_heritage: Several small landers and orbiters (e.g. Beresheet, Hakuto-R, IM-1, Blue Ghost, Danuri) - from general knowledge, not re-checked

launchers.name: New Glenn
launchers.config: 7x2 (seven BE-4, two BE-3U), reusable first stage
launchers.status_note: 3 launches (Jan 2025, Nov 2025, 19 Apr 2026). The third left its payload in an off-nominal orbit (upper-stage problem). On 28 May 2026 a vehicle exploded during a static-fire test and heavily damaged the launch site; no flight since. The Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander launch is listed no earlier than Q1 2027. A larger 9x4 variant (>70 t LEO, >20 t TLI) is in development and not included here.
launchers.tli_note: 7x2 configuration: 7 t to TLI (Blue Origin figure as quoted by Wikipedia).

launchers.name: Vulcan Centaur
launchers.config: VC6: six GEM 63XL solid boosters, Centaur V
launchers.status_note: 4 launches (2024 - Feb 2026). Grounded for nine months after a solid-booster nozzle failure on the Feb 2026 flight. The return to flight, which is also the first six-booster (VC6) launch, was scheduled for 13 Nov 2026 and slipped by a day or two; its outcome could NOT be verified when this file was written (15 Nov 2026). Smaller configurations: VC0 2.3 t, VC2 6.3 t, VC4 9.2 t to TLI.
launchers.height_note: standard fairing; 67.3 m with the long fairing
launchers.tli_note: VC6: 11,500 kg to TLI (ULA web page table).
launchers.lunar_heritage: Peregrine Mission One (Jan 2024, VC2) - from general knowledge, not re-checked

launchers.name: Ariane 6
launchers.status_note: 9 Ariane 6 launches since Jul 2024 (8 successes, 1 partial failure on the maiden flight). First four-booster A64 flight on 12 Feb 2026; three A64 flights in 2026 so far, all successful.
launchers.tli_note: A64: 8,600 kg to lunar transfer orbit (operator figure as quoted by Wikipedia's infobox, listed as 'LTO').

launchers.name: Long March 10
launchers.config: three-core lunar version (core + 2 boosters, three stages)
launchers.status_note: China's crewed-lunar launcher. The full three-core vehicle has not flown; its first flight (uncrewed Mengzhou to TLI) is listed for 2027. Single-core relatives have flown: a suborbital Long March 10A test with a Mengzhou abort test on 11 Feb 2026, and the Long March 10B, which reached orbit in mid-2026 (10 Jul 2026 per Wikipedia; another outlet's headline dates a maiden flight to about 1 May - not reconciled).
launchers.tli_note: Design figure: at least 27 t to TLI (as quoted by Wikipedia). Not demonstrated.

launchers.name: Long March 5
launchers.config: CZ-5 (two-stage core + 4 boosters); not the LEO-only CZ-5B
launchers.status_note: 11 CZ-5 launches (10 successes, 1 failure); latest 11 Jun 2026. Launched the Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 sample-return missions.
launchers.leo_note: no LEO figure for CZ-5; the 25 t figure belongs to the CZ-5B variant
launchers.tli_note: 8.8-9.4 t to TLI quoted by Wikipedia; the lower end is used here.
launchers.lunar_heritage: Chang'e 5 (2020); Chang'e 6 (2024) - the latter from general knowledge, not re-checked

launchers.name: LVM3
launchers.config: two S200 solid boosters, L110 core, C25 cryogenic upper stage
launchers.status_note: 9 launches, all successful (count as of Dec 2025 per Wikipedia; later flights not checked). Chandrayaan-3 (3,900 kg) was not sent straight to TLI: LVM3 left it in a 170 x 36,500 km Earth orbit and the spacecraft raised its own orbit and performed TLI about 17 days later (landing 40 days after launch).
launchers.tli_note: 3,000 kg to TLI as quoted by Wikipedia's infobox (the GTO-scaling estimate gives 2.9 t).

launchers.name: H3
launchers.config: H3-24L: two LE-9 engines, four SRB-3 boosters, long fairing
launchers.status_note: 9 launches, 7 successes, 2 failures (Mar 2023 maiden flight; 22 Dec 2025). Returned to flight on 12 Jun 2026; latest launch 10 Aug 2026. Only one flight so far used the H3-24 configuration (Oct 2025).
launchers.leo_note: to ISS orbit, as quoted by Wikipedia
launchers.tli_note: H3-24: more than 6,000 kg to TLI as quoted by Wikipedia; JAXA's own document was not opened.

launchers.name: Soyuz-2.1b / Fregat
launchers.status_note: Flying regularly (latest 2.1b/Fregat-M flight checked: 24 Aug 2026). Launched Luna 25 on 10 Aug 2023 (launch succeeded; the lander was later lost).
launchers.tli_note: 2,350 kg to TLI as quoted by Wikipedia.

launchers.name: Angara A5
launchers.config: five URM-1 cores, URM-2, Briz-M upper stage
launchers.status_note: 5 launches (4 successes, 1 partial failure); latest found 19 Jun 2025 - flights after that were not checked.
launchers.tli_note: UNVERIFIED: no TLI figure found. Low-confidence estimate by GTO scaling from 5.4 t to GTO with Briz-M, assuming 2.4 t stage dry mass and Isp 326 s (assumptions) -> about 3.9 t. The published GTO figure includes a large plane change from high-latitude Plesetsk, so the real TLI capability may be higher.

launchers.name: Neutron
launchers.config: expendable (15 t LEO); 13 t with downrange booster landing
launchers.status_note: First launch slipped to 2027 (no earlier than Q2 2027 per Wikipedia; delay reported Oct 2026).
launchers.tli_note: UNVERIFIED: no lunar figure published. Lower bound only: 1,500 kg is the published capability to Mars/Venus, which needs more energy than TLI, so the TLI capability is at least this.

launchers.name: Electron
launchers.config: two stages to LEO; the spacecraft's own stage must do TLI
launchers.status_note: 99 launches since 2017 (95 successes, 4 failures) per Wikipedia. Sent the CAPSTONE cubesat to the Moon in 2022 using a Photon kick stage; Wikipedia quotes up to about 30 kg into lunar orbit with Photon. No direct TLI capability.
launchers.tli_note: Delivers 300 kg to LEO only. This tool adds a TLI burn by the spacecraft's own stage at the entered Isp and compares the resulting mass in LEO with 300 kg.

launchers.name: Saturn V
launchers.config: three stages (S-IC, S-II, S-IVB) - shown for scale only
launchers.status_note: 13 launches, 9 Nov 1967 - 14 May 1973. Retired: included only as a size and capability reference for the Apollo landings.
launchers.tli_note: 43,500 kg to TLI as quoted by Wikipedia.
launchers.lunar_heritage: Apollo lunar missions, 1968-1972 (general knowledge, not re-checked)
